module_title: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) vs. CrPC: Foundational Concepts
introduction: This foundational level introduces the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), which replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC). It focuses on the structural changes, the formalization of digital procedures, and the revolutionary changes to the FIR process.

core_concepts.title: Structural Overhaul
core_concepts.description:
The BNSS modernizes procedural criminal law, heavily integrating technology.
- Sections: The CrPC had 484 sections; the BNSS has 531 sections.
- Timeline: Came into force on July 1, 2024. Any FIR registered on or after this date will follow BNSS procedures, while pending trials continue under CrPC.

core_concepts.title: Zero FIR (Section 173 BNSS)
core_concepts.description:
Under the CrPC, 'Zero FIR' was a judicial creation (based on the Justice Verma Committee report after Nirbhaya) but lacked explicit statutory backing. 
- BNSS Codification: Section 173 explicitly mandates that a police officer MUST register an FIR irrespective of the area where the offense was committed. It is assigned a 'Zero' number and later transferred to the police station with actual jurisdiction.

core_concepts.title: e-FIR (Electronic FIR)
core_concepts.description:
BNSS legally recognizes the filing of an FIR through electronic communication. 
- Caveat: To prevent frivolous digital complaints, the electronic information must be physically signed by the informant within **3 days** for it to be formally registered as an FIR.

core_concepts.title: Preliminary Enquiry Formalized (Section 173(3) BNSS)
core_concepts.description:
For offenses punishable with 3 to 7 years of imprisonment, the police are now legally allowed to conduct a 'Preliminary Enquiry' before registering an FIR. 
- Purpose: To ascertain whether a prima facie (at first sight) case exists. 
- Time limit: Must be completed within **14 days**. (This codifies the Supreme Court's ruling in the Lalita Kumari case).

important_entities.name: Deemed Sanction for Prosecution
important_entities.key_fact: A strict 120-day limit for the Government to decide on prosecuting civil servants.
important_entities.significance: Under the CrPC, governments would often sit on files for years, refusing to give 'sanction' to prosecute corrupt officials. The BNSS mandates that if the government does not decide within 120 days, the sanction is *deemed* to be given, and the trial can proceed.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Did the BNSS change the sentencing power of Magistrates? Yes. Under CrPC, a Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM) could impose a fine of any amount, and a Magistrate of First Class (JMFC) could impose up to Rs 10,000. BNSS Section 23 updates this: JMFCs can now impose fines up to Rs 50,000, and Magistrates of Second Class up to Rs 10,000.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: An e-FIR must be signed in 3 days. A preliminary enquiry must end in 14 days.

exam_strategy_tips: If a CLAT or Judiciary question asks 'Which newly codified concept in the BNSS legally mandates police to register an offense outside their territorial jurisdiction?', the answer is **Zero FIR**.
